{"self_assessment": "**Impact**
Our table built a fish: a body outline that splits from the nose, with a forked tail. By the last check, about 100 of the 111 standing dominoes were connected to the start. My share was the lower tail fork, plus a redo of the upper fork at the tail joint, which was the one spot that stayed pale for a long time. I also spotted the stray pale line running down from the nose, which was not in the sketch. Tom and Priya cleared it, which kept the outline clean. I can't see how the push turned out, so I can't say whether the judge recognized the fish. The outline looked right to me beforehand.

**Execution**
I laid the lower tail from the pad stroke and it went dark. When the upper fork stayed pale, I judged the gap too big to nudge, lifted the stroke and laid it fresh from the joint. It was still pale after that, so I inspected the joint to find out why. It then turned out dark to the tip. The joint is crowded where the two lines cross. I judged it connected and left it alone rather than risk bumping it. One correction: at 9:30 I told Tom I had not fixed the joint, which was too narrow. I did relay the upper fork earlier. After that I only inspected and left it alone.

**Collaboration**
I said out loud what I was touching so Tom and I did not collide at the tail, and I kept my hands off the nose, which was Priya's. I flagged the nose joint and the stray line to the right people instead of fixing them myself. When Tom's credit for me was wrong, I corrected it.

**Leadership**
I did not lead the plan. Maya ran the sketch and the split of work, and Priya and Tom coordinated the nose and the cleanup. I took my stroke, owned the tail joint problem and kept the record accurate. I could have offered more help during the long hands-off stretch."}
